name: Otoplasty (ear pinning)

lead: Otoplasty reshapes or repositions the cartilage of the outer ear. For prominent ears it is usually done by creating or restoring the fold of the antihelix, reducing a deep conchal bowl, or repositioning a protruding lobe. The aim is to bring the ear closer to the head.

In looksmaxxing forums it is often described as a high-return, relatively low-cost add-on, and some members say prominent ears can undermine otherwise balanced facial features. Reviews in the surgical literature describe high patient satisfaction, but note that no single technique is considered definitive.

paras: Surgeons either use stitches that bend the cartilage into a fold without cutting it, score or cut the cartilage so it bends back, or remove a portion of the conchal cartilage. Some centres also describe closed, needle-based or minimally invasive versions. A head band is typically worn for several weeks afterwards to protect the shape.

Documented complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, scarring, recurrence of prominence and overcorrection with an unnatural contour. A large case review of 562 patients reported significant morbidity including residual deformity. Forum members also discuss revision surgery for lobe or helix irregularities. Surgery is an Rx medical procedure performed by licensed surgeons.

lead: Otoplasty, commonly called ear pinning, is plastic surgery of the outer ear (auricle). It is most often performed to correct prominent ears, sometimes called "bat ears", which result from an underdeveloped antihelical fold, an enlarged conchal bowl, or a protruding earlobe. [1][2] The same family of operations is also used for congenital malformations such as constricted ears, Stahl's deformity and cryptotia, and for ear reconstruction. [3][4]

Surgical reviews describe prominent ears as the most common abnormality of the external ear, and note that more than 200 different techniques have been described. [5][6] One 2005 review concluded there is no clearly definitive technique, while another noted that despite the variety patient satisfaction is generally high. [3][5] Evidence for otoplasty consists mainly of case series, retrospective comparisons and expert reviews rather than large controlled trials.

In looksmaxxing communities otoplasty is discussed as a small but visible surgical add-on, frequently mentioned alongside jaw surgery and rhinoplasty. [7] Members debate its payoff, its ideal timing and the risk of ending up with ears that look "pinned". [8][9]
infobox: Prominent ears; congenital or acquired ear deformities
Local or general, depending on age and technique
Mustarde sutures, Furnas conchamastoid sutures, Stenstrom scoring, closed methods

paras: The auricle is a cartilage framework covered by thin skin. Prominence typically arises from a missing or shallow antihelical fold, an overly deep concha, a protruding lobule, or a combination. [1][10] Beyond prominent ears, otoplasty techniques are used for constricted ears, Stahl's deformity, cryptotia and macrotia. [3][4]
Reviews note that the physical consequences of prominent ears are minor, while the aesthetic and psychological effects can be substantial. [3]

Surgical approaches are commonly grouped into those that keep the cartilage intact and use sutures to create a fold, those that score or cut the cartilage so it bends, and those that remove cartilage to reduce projection. [10] Named methods include Mustarde mattress sutures, Furnas conchamastoid sutures, Stenstrom anterior scoring, and the closed Merck stitch method. [10]

One review describes mattress sutures to create an antihelical fold as offering benefits that outweigh their risks, and conservative resection of the concha for prominent conchal bowls; it also states that a surgeon should be comfortable with several techniques. [2] Surgeon opinion papers describe differing preferences between cartilage-cutting and cartilage-sparing approaches. [11]

Minimally invasive and closed techniques have also been reported, including a German series of 385 ears corrected by a closed technique, and later reviews of minimally invasive otoplasty. [12][13] An implantable clip system has been evaluated in a pilot study. [14]

Wikipedia notes that surgery for prominent ears may be carried out from about age four to six, once the ear is close to adult size, and that general anesthesia is often used in children. [10] A Grokipedia summary reports surgery typically around ages 4 to 6. [15]

Adults can also be treated; community posts note that some surgeons are reluctant to operate on teenagers because of scarring concerns, a claim made by forum members rather than established in the reviewed literature. [9]
In newborns, non-surgical ear molding with tape or splints is described as feasible during the first weeks of life while cartilage remains pliable. [10]
A bulky dressing is typically worn for several days, followed by a snug headband worn at night for roughly three to six weeks. Swelling and bruising usually subside within about two weeks. [10]

A literature review of complication rates found that over 200 techniques exist but relatively few articles report complication rates; early complications included hematoma and infection. [16] A review of 562 consecutive cases reported significant morbidity, including residual deformity, hemorrhage, infection, keloid or hypertrophic scarring and anterior skin necrosis. [17]

Wikipedia lists hematoma, infection (including perichondritis), suture extrusion, skin necrosis from tight dressings, and overcorrection with unnatural contour. [10] Surgical authors have suggested that technical errors, rather than springy cartilage, account for many failed primary procedures. [2]

On looksmax.org, members describe concerns such as outward-turned lobes, a downward-pointing upper helix and extra folds after pinning, and discuss revision otoplasty. [8] These are personal accounts, not systematic data.

Human studies of otoplasty are largely case series and surgical comparisons. A randomized comparison of rasps versus puncture needles for creating an antihelical fold has been published, as has a study comparing a standard and a modified Chong-Chet technique with long-term follow-up. [18][19]

A controlled study examined ear sensibility after otoplasty, and a study of 62 children and adults using suture techniques reported improvements in health-related quality of life and patient benefit. [20][21] A German series of 385 ears corrected with a closed technique reported on a large number of patients. [12] A 2016 pilot study evaluated an implantable clip system. [14]

A review of 562 consecutive cases documented complication rates including residual deformity needing revision. [17] No large randomized trial has compared otoplasty with no surgery for appearance outcomes in adults seeking facial improvement.

Among looksmaxxing forum users, otoplasty is described as an inexpensive add-on compared with jaw surgery; one poster called it a "high roi" option, while another replied that neither rhinoplasty nor otoplasty was important. [7] One thread claims it can boost facial masculinity more than custom implants, which is a community opinion that has not been tested. [8]
A 2019 study of Google search interest in facial cosmetic procedures is among the public-interest analyses that include ear surgery. [22]
